title: Formless, beyond compare
hookLine: arupe hain, anupe hain: without form, beyond comparison (Jaap, chachari)

lines: BETTER THAN, WORSE THAN, NOT AS.
THE MIND IS A MEASURING MACHINE.
SOMETHING NOTHING CAN BE SET BESIDE.
cards: Better than yesterday. Worse than her. Not as tall, as fast, as rich, as liked.
The mind is a measuring machine. It can hardly look at anything without setting it beside something else and checking which is bigger. A sunset gets compared to last week's.
A child gets compared to a cousin. A few minutes of scrolling, and the comparisons pile up. Then a hymn says, in two words, that there is something nothing can be set beside.

teach.b: Further on, Jaap moves into a meter called chachari, and its lines are startlingly short: two words each. Aroop hain. Anoop hain.
Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. After the snake's long glide, it feels like quick footsteps, or a heartbeat.
Hain means You are, so each line is a tiny sentence. Today, the first two, which the glide already saluted as aroope and anoope.
Aroop: roop is form, shape, appearance, and the small a means without. You are formless. Nobody can paint You, sculpt You, put You on a screen.
Sikhs take this seriously: there are no statues of God in a gurdwara, and the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, sits where you might expect an image.
Then anoop, from upma, comparison, likeness: the One with nothing to compare to. The two words lean on each other. Comparison needs shapes.
To say this is bigger than that, you need a this and a that, each with an outline. With no form, there's nothing to measure against.
Beyond compare isn't a boast that God wins every contest.

So every morning, before the comparing starts, a Sikh reciting Jaap spends a few seconds saluting the one thing that can't be ranked: a small rest for the mind, where better than and worse than simply don't apply.

how: Sikhs recite the short chachari lines of Jaap Sahib briskly each morning, and gurdwaras keep no images of God: the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, is the center.

o: without any form or shape to picture
hidden, so eyes can never see it
vague, with no clear qualities at all

games.q: formless, beyond compare — tap the pairs.

s: beyond compare means God wins every contest
with no form there's nothing to measure against: no contest at all.
gurdwaras keep no statues or images of God
the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, sits at the center.
the chachari lines of Jaap are long and slow
each line is just two words: aroop hain, anoop hain.

games.q: your mind keeps measuring: better than, worse than. Jaap says the One is aroop and anoop. why can't the One be compared?
o: because the One always comes first.
because comparing needs shapes, and the One has no form.
games.why: aroop, formless, and anoop, beyond compare, lean on each other: with no outline, there's nothing to set beside.

practice: Look at one thing in front of you, a cup, a plant, your own hand, the sky in the window, and let it be just this.
Each time the mind says nicer than, older than, not as good as, smile at it and come back: not better, not worse, here. If you pray, you can say aroop hain, anoop hain softly.

wordCard.voice: Formless. Aroop hain, anoop hain: You are without form, and beyond compare, in the short, quick lines of Jaap's chachari meter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: aroop, without form, from roop, form or appearance.

carryVoice: Your line: beyond compare. With no shape, there's nothing to measure the One against. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Jaap Sahib, chachari chhand (from stanza 29): aroop hain, anoop hain
